title: Do Heavy Tails Help Diffusion? On the Subtle Trade-off Between Initialization and Training
claim: Heavy-tailed noise models do not uniformly reduce tail error; trained-network error grows at extreme quantiles and can offset the initialization advantage.
layout: 2x2 grid of line plots, shared legend below, per-panel dataset captions
description: A 2x2 grid of line plots. Each plots Coordinate TCE (y-axis) against reference quantile (x-axis, log-scaled from 1-10^-1 toward extreme tail values like 1-10^-5). Panels are (a) isotropic alpha-stable, (b) unbalanced alpha-stable mixture, (c) HRRR East wet hours, and (d) wildfire size. Each panel has several colored curves with markers. Open markers show zero networks and filled markers show trained models. Methods are DLPM, t-EDM, linear Gaussian flow, DDPM-V and DDIM-V, plus a dashed gray test-test baseline near zero. Several curves climb steeply at the extreme tail and are clipped, marked 'High values clipped'. The blue DLPM zero curve rises steadily. A shared two-column legend sits below the panels. The eye goes first to the blue and red curves that shoot upward.
caption: Coordinate TCE versus reference quantile. Open markers denote zero networks; gray is test-test. High values are clipped where marked. Tail ranges follow [ref].
abstract: Recent works have proposed incorporating heavy-tailed (HT) noise into diffusion- and flow-based generative models, with the goals of better recovering the tails of target distributions and improving generative diversity. This motivation is intuitive: if the data are heavy-tailed, HT noise may appear better matched than light-tailed (LT) Gaussian noise. However, replacing Gaussian noise by HT noise also changes the underlying estimation problem. In this paper, we revisit this paradigm through a combined theoretical and empirical study, establishing sampling-error bounds for two representative diffusion models driven by HT and LT noise. We show that HT diffusion models can achieve exponentially fast initialization, but accumulated training errors may offset this advantage. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support our theoretical findings. Our results call into question a growing design trend in generative modeling and challenge the use of HT noise to improve rare-region exploration.
